name: Chocho de Santa Catarina Ocotlán
catalog_citation: Mock, Carol. 1977. Chocho de Santa Catarina Ocotlán, Oaxaca. Archivo de Lenguas Indígenas de México 4. México: El Colegio de México.
catalog_quote: Acento. Cada palabra tiene una sílaba tónica, generalmente la penúltima, en cuyo caso no la marcamos en la ortografía. Cuando el acento cae en otra sílaba, se marca con /ˈ/ ante la sílaba acentuada. acento en la penúltima: kąθē 'palma' ... acento final: kàˈnià 'petate'

new_statements.quote: Acento. Cada palabra tiene una sílaba tónica, generalmente la penúltima, en cuyo caso no la marcamos en la ortografía. Cuando el acento cae en otra sílaba, se marca con ' ante la sílaba acentuada. acento en la penúltima: [ka.e] 'palma'; acento final: [ka'nia] 'petate'. [p. 28:] Las vocales sencillas /i e ɛ a ɔ o u ɨ/ se alargan en sílaba tónica final de palabra o ante consonante débil /b d g z ž r l/.
new_statements.translation: Accent. Every word has one stressed syllable, generally the penultimate, in which case we do not mark it in the orthography. When the accent falls on another syllable, it is marked with ' before the stressed syllable. penultimate accent: 'palm'; final accent: 'reed mat'. [p. 28:] The simple vowels lengthen in a word-final stressed syllable or before a weak consonant.

new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: extracted text page 23 (printed p. 25): 'Acento / Cada palabra tiene una silaba tOnica, generalmente la penultima, en cuyo caso no la marcamos en la ortografia. Cuando el acento cae en otra silaba, se marca con,',' ante la silaba acentuada. / acento en la peratima' kaee 'palm* / acento final: ka*nie 'petate' — the Spanish matches the quote with accents restored; the Chocho forms are scanned-garbled as the reader said. The same page lists six 'Tonos': alto, medio, bajo, alto descendente, medio ascendente, bajo ascendente. Page 26 (printed p. 28), item 5: 'Las vocales sencillas /i e ɛ a ɔ o u ɨ/ se alargan en silaba tonica final de palabra o ante consonante debil /b d g z ž r l/' — confirmed.…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's penultimate rule (penultimate stress) for the default case; refines it by stating that stress is only 'generally' penultimate, that final-stressed words occur and are lexically marked, and that the language is simultaneously tonal (six tones). This source is the 1977 Archivo de Lenguas Indígenas volume for the very same town as the catalog entry, found on archive.org (ERIC) while searching for the listed works; it is offered as an additional open source, not as one of the three assigned works.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stressed syllable per word, by default the penult; a minority of words are stressed on the final syllable and these are marked lexically in the orthography with a preceding apostrophe. The language also has six lexical tones (high, mid, low, high-falling, mid-rising, low-rising) listed on the same page, so stress coexists with tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stressed words exist and are orthographically marked (example 'petate'); the p. 28 rule that simple vowels lengthen in a word-final stressed syllable confirms final stress is a real position.
new_statements.identity_note: Veerman-Leichsenring 2000 and the extra 1977 Archivo volume describe the Santa Catarina Ocotlán variety (the catalog's entry). Grosser Lerner 2000 describes Chocho of Santa María Nativitas, Coixtlahuaca, a different town's variety; d'Ascanio 2012 is a state-of-knowledge survey of Chocho in general, not tied to one town.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page image we hold of Mock 1977 p. 25; it is the entire accent statement in the book (scanned search of all 154 held pages). (2) The deciding source is a 1977 ALIM questionnaire sketch by a professional linguist, held in full; the classification (penultimate default, weight-blind, lexically marked exceptions incl. final stress) follows directly from it. sources.quote: No statement of stress position for Chocho. Says stress is contrastive/penultimate in Metzontla Popoloc (Veerman-Leichsenring 1991: 36-38: '(CV)CVCV pattern with stress on the penultimate vowel') and that 'Veerman-Leichsenring (2000b: 321-322) argues that Popoloc, Chocho, and Ixcatec also have stress in monosyllabic words, phonetically realized as vowel gemination, disyllabic realization of a diphthong or through the addition of an affix as a prothetic vowel.' Mazatec stress final.
